topic.title: Money and markets
topic.description: Use short cases to see how money and markets work.

concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.hook: Five ₹20 idlis fit a ₹100 note; after each idli becomes ₹25, only four fit. The note has not changed. What did?
concepts.rule: Inflation is a rise in the broad price level. If cash stays the same while prices rise, that cash buys less. A price jump for one snack alone is not the whole index.

claims.text: India uses a consumer price index to track change in a basket of retail prices.
A rise in broad prices cuts the buying power of cash if its amount stays fixed.

items.stem: At the hostel canteen, a ₹100 note once covered five ₹20 idlis. Each now costs ₹25. How many fit?

options.text: Four idlis.
options.feedback: The note is fixed while each serving costs more; one serving drops out of the budget.

options.text: Five idlis.
options.feedback: That count assumes the old price still applies, even though the canteen now asks for more per plate.

items.stem: During exam week, Meera's tea price doubles but most other prices stay flat. Does that prove broad inflation doubled?

options.text: No; one price is not the basket.
options.feedback: The index follows many items, so a sharp tea price jump need not match the broad change.

options.text: Yes; tea sets the whole index.
options.feedback: A single canteen item cannot stand in for the full mix of goods that households buy.

items.stem: A broad basket costs ₹100, then ₹125 after inflation. If cash stays at ₹100, about what percent of the original basket can it now buy?

options.feedback: The same cash now covers four fifths of the unchanged basket, showing lower purchasing power.
That is the new price relative to the old one, not the basket share fixed cash buys.

items.stem: A family shop raises only mango prices after a poor crop. Which claim fits the price index?

options.text: The mango change alone cannot show broad inflation.
options.feedback: An index combines many prices, which can move in different directions from one crop.

options.text: Every item in the index rose equally.
options.feedback: A crop shock tells us about mangoes; it does not say what happened to all other goods.

items.stem: Bus fares rise while most other prices stay flat. Why can a fixed scholarship buy fewer rides without proving broad inflation?

options.text: One fare changed, not the whole price basket.
options.feedback: The ride budget shrinks, but inflation is about a broad index rather than one fare.

options.text: Fewer affordable rides prove every price rose.
options.feedback: A single fare can cut one kind of purchasing power without describing the rest of the basket.

items.stem: Fill the gap: compare ₹100 with a basket costing ₹100, then with the same basket costing ₹110. The cash now covers ___.

options.text: Less than one full basket.
options.feedback: A higher basket price lowers what unchanged cash covers; this is the purchasing power link.

options.text: More than one full basket.
options.feedback: That would require the basket to cost less than the cash, while its new price is higher.

items.stem: Samosas, tea and idlis all cost more at one canteen. A student says the national price index rose by the same share. What is the gap?

options.text: One canteen is not the full basket.
options.feedback: A few foods at one shop cannot show how prices changed across the whole country.

options.text: Three rising foods are enough to set the whole index.
options.feedback: The index also includes many other goods, services and places with different price changes.

items.stem: Put the two events in order for fixed cash to lose buying power.

options.text: First: the basket price rises.
options.feedback: The price change comes before the fixed amount covers a smaller share of that basket.

options.text: Second: fixed cash buys less of that basket.
options.feedback: This follows the higher price; putting it first would hide the cause of the loss.

misconceptions.name: One price is the index
misconceptions.correction: One snack can rise while the broad basket moves in a different way.

misconceptions.name: Same cash, same goods
misconceptions.correction: When broad prices rise, the same cash can buy fewer goods.

sources.title: Consumer Price Index and inflation rate for students
sources.publisher: Sankhyiki, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.hook: ₹1 lakh growing at a made-up 7% for 30 years becomes about ₹7.6 lakh. The last ten years add more than the first twenty.
concepts.rule: Compounding means a gain can earn a later gain when it stays in the pot. A SIP adds money at set times, but that does not promise a set return.

claims.text: Compound growth includes growth on past gains as well as the starting amount.
A SIP is a way to add money at set times; market returns are not fixed.

items.stem: In a family shop ledger, Riya leaves ₹100 interest beside ₹1,000. At the same rate, what earns interest next?

options.text: Both the start amount and the saved interest.
options.feedback: Once a gain stays in the account, later growth can apply to that larger total.

options.text: Only the original ₹1,000.
options.feedback: That leaves out the gain still sitting in the balance, which can itself earn a later gain.

items.stem: A hostel club keeps each year's fund gain in its account. A second club removes every gain. Which balance can grow faster at one fixed rate?

options.text: The club that keeps its gains.
options.feedback: Its later percentage acts on earlier gains as well as the starting amount.

options.text: The club that removes every gain.
options.feedback: Taking gains out leaves the base unchanged, so later gains lack that added layer.

items.stem: A toy account starts at ₹100 and gains 10% in year one. It keeps that gain. Under compounding at the same rate, about how many rupees of gain arrive in year two?

options.feedback: The second gain applies to ₹110 because the first gain stayed in the account.
That repeats the first gain and misses interest earned on the retained ₹10.

items.stem: An exam club adds ₹100 each month to a fund. Which part is a payment pattern, rather than a return promise?

options.text: The repeated monthly addition.
options.feedback: The schedule says when money enters; it cannot set what markets later pay.

options.text: A guaranteed monthly profit.
options.feedback: Money added at set times can still face changing market prices and uncertain returns.

items.stem: Two toy accounts start equal at the same steady positive rate. One keeps gains, the other removes them. Why can the first add more later?

options.text: Retained gains enter the next rate base.
options.feedback: The same percentage applies to a larger balance when earlier gains remain in the account.

options.text: The stated rate must increase each year.
options.feedback: A steady rate can produce larger rupee gains because the balance it acts on grows.

items.stem: A toy account grows from ₹200 to ₹220. If the ₹20 stays, the next year's 10% is taken from ___.

options.feedback: The saved gain has joined the base, which is the key step in compounding.
That would ignore the money left in the account after the first gain.

items.stem: A chart compounds a fixed 10% each year, then a student predicts the same path for a real share. What assumption slipped in?

options.text: Real returns need not stay positive or fixed.
options.feedback: The toy calculation assumes a stable gain, while an actual share can change value in either direction.

options.text: Compounding needs a monthly deposit to work.
options.feedback: Kept gains can grow without fresh cash. The flaw is treating future gains as sure.

items.stem: Match each label to its role in a toy account.

options.text: Starting ₹100
options.feedback: This sum came first. It is the base on which the first gain is worked out.

options.text: Base for the first gain
options.feedback: The first base is present before any gain has been added to the account.

options.text: Saved ₹10 gain
options.feedback: This gain stays in the account, so it can join the amount used for the next gain.

options.text: Part of the next base
options.feedback: The later rate can act on this saved gain as well as the first sum.

misconceptions.name: Gain only on start
misconceptions.correction: When gains stay in the pot, later gains can build on them too.

misconceptions.name: SIP means sure gain
misconceptions.correction: A SIP sets a payment pattern; it does not set market returns.

concepts.title: The rule of 72
concepts.hook: At a made-up 9% rate, 72 ÷ 9 says eight years to double. The exact compound calculation lands close, but not on eight.
concepts.rule: For a steady percent gain, divide 72 by the rate to guess the years to double. It is a rough math shortcut, not a promise of market growth.

claims.text: The rule of 72 is a rough way to guess when a sum may double. Divide 72 by a set rate.
Market returns do not have a fixed rate, so the shortcut is only a what-if tool there.

items.stem: A hostel quiz shows a steady 8% toy growth rate. What doubling time does the rule of 72 suggest?

options.text: About nine years.
options.feedback: The shortcut divides 72 by eight, then treats the answer as a rough time.

options.text: Exactly eight years.
options.feedback: Eight is the rate in this case; the estimate comes from dividing 72 by it.

items.stem: On a train, Arjun compares two made-up constant rates: 6% and 9%. Which has the shorter rough doubling time?

options.text: The 9% case.
options.feedback: A larger assumed rate makes 72 divided by that rate smaller.

options.text: The 6% case.
options.feedback: A smaller rate takes more periods to build the same doubling under the shortcut.

items.stem: A toy account was growing at a steady 6%, then its steady rate falls to 3%. Using the rule of 72, about how many years would doubling take at the new rate?

options.text: 24 years.
options.feedback: The lower steady rate gives a longer rough doubling time; the shortcut uses the new rate.

options.text: 12 years.
options.feedback: That uses the old six percent rate even though the account now grows at three percent.

items.stem: A class chart shows a market rate that changes each year. How should its rule-of-72 answer be read?

options.text: As a rough what-if under a steady rate.
options.feedback: The shortcut assumes one rate, so a changing path may reach double at another time.

options.text: As a guaranteed doubling date.
options.feedback: Market changes can shift the path, so a single assumed percentage cannot fix a date.

items.stem: A toy balance grows steadily at 12%, another at 4%. Why does the rule of 72 give different doubling times?

options.text: A higher steady rate needs fewer years.
options.feedback: Dividing 72 by a larger rate gives a shorter rough time, assuming each rate stays steady.

options.text: The faster account must have started with more money.
options.feedback: Starting balance is not part of this shortcut; the assumed percentage rate drives the time.

items.stem: At a fixed 3% toy rate, the rule gives 72 ÷ 3 = ___.

options.text: About 24 years.
options.feedback: A low rate makes the doubling estimate long; the rule still gives only an approximation.

options.text: About 3 years.
options.feedback: That repeats the rate as years and misses the much larger quotient from the division.

items.stem: A savings rate is 8% this year and 4% next year. A student says 72 ÷ 8 proves a nine-year doubling date. What is the flaw?

options.text: The shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.
options.feedback: A changing rate breaks the simple input, and even a steady-rate result would be approximate.

options.text: The shortcut works only for a one-year balance.
options.feedback: The rule estimates years to double under a steady rate, not a guaranteed date from one year.

items.stem: Which line best explains why this shortcut is useful in a classroom?

options.text: It turns a rate into a quick doubling guess.
options.feedback: You can do this sum in your head. A full growth sum may give a different time.

options.text: It proves a market return will stay fixed.
options.feedback: A fast guess does not make a real rate stay the same each year.

misconceptions.name: Exact clock
misconceptions.correction: The rule gives a rough guess, not an exact date.

misconceptions.name: Any market rate is fixed
misconceptions.correction: Market gains can vary; the shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.

concepts.title: Risk and return
concepts.hook: A fair coin pays ₹30 on heads and nothing on tails; a sure ₹12 ticket pays less at best but never zero. The range matters.
concepts.rule: A bigger possible gain often comes with more chance of loss or a wider range of results. A high possible return is not a sure return.

claims.text: Investment risk includes the chance of loss and uncertain results.
A high possible gain may mean more risk. The gain is not sure.

items.stem: At a school fair, a game pays ₹30 or ₹0. A second game pays ₹12 for sure. Which result range is wider?

options.text: The first game's range.
options.feedback: Its two possible payoffs are far apart, so its outcome is less certain.

options.text: The sure game's range.
options.feedback: A fixed payoff has no spread between best and worst outcomes in this simple setup.

items.stem: During exam week, a family shop pays to make a new snack that may sell out or go unsold. Which outcome is possible?

options.text: A loss as well as a gain.
options.feedback: Some snacks may not sell. A big best case does not tell us how many buyers will come.

options.text: Only a gain, since the best case is large.
options.feedback: A strong best case does not remove the weaker outcome if buyers do not appear.

items.stem: A raffle ticket costs ₹30. One of four equal tickets pays ₹100 and the others pay nothing. About what is the average net return per ticket, including the ticket cost?

options.text: A loss of ₹5.
options.feedback: The average payout is ₹25, below the ₹30 cost, even though one outcome pays ₹100.

options.text: A gain of ₹70.
options.feedback: That is the best single result after cost, not the average across all four outcomes.

items.stem: A poster shows only its best possible payout. What key part of risk is missing?

options.text: The chance and size of poor outcomes.
options.feedback: A maximum alone leaves out how often that amount occurs and what losses remain possible.

options.text: The colour of the poster.
options.feedback: Design does not reveal the range of payoffs or the chance of losing money.

items.stem: A share poster says its price could gain 30%, but gives no other outcomes or their chances. Why is its average return unknown?

options.text: One possible gain is not the full outcome set.
options.feedback: To find an average, we need the other possible gains and losses, plus their chances.

options.text: Holding longer makes the quoted gain the average.
options.feedback: Time alone does not turn a possible upside into a known expected return.

items.stem: Complete the comparison: ₹10 for sure has a narrow range; ₹0 or ₹30 has a ___.

options.text: Wider range of outcomes.
options.feedback: The second payoff can land at either extreme, making its result less predictable.

options.text: Guaranteed larger payoff.
options.feedback: One branch gives nothing, so the larger headline amount is not assured.

items.stem: Two games have the same average payout, but one has much wider results. A student says the wider game must pay more. What is wrong?

options.text: A wider range can bring lower outcomes too.
options.feedback: More variation changes the risk of each result; it does not raise the stated average by itself.

options.text: A wider range removes the chance of a loss.
options.feedback: The low end can fall further even when the average stays the same.

items.stem: Which sentence captures the trade in this fair-game example?

options.text: The larger possible prize comes with more spread.
options.feedback: Comparing both good and bad outcomes shows what the attractive headline hides.

options.text: The largest prize is the only outcome that counts.
options.feedback: The zero prize can happen too. Leave it out and the game's range looks false.

misconceptions.name: High means sure
misconceptions.correction: A high possible return can come with a loss too.

misconceptions.name: No loss is possible
misconceptions.correction: An uncertain asset can lose value as well as gain it.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.hook: A monsoon cancels cricket practice and hurts both a bat seller and a ball seller. Two products can still share one shock.
concepts.rule: Spreading money across different holdings can cut the harm from one weak part. It cannot make all loss go away, since many parts can fall together.

claims.text: A mix of holdings can spread the risk from one firm.
A broad mix can cut some risk from one firm. It cannot wipe out all risk.

items.stem: A family shop sells only mango juice. Monsoon rain cuts foot traffic. What happens to its sales mix?

options.text: Its only sale line bears the whole stall shock.
options.feedback: With one product, there is no other product line to offset that lost demand.

options.text: The shop is shielded by selling one item.
options.feedback: Concentration ties the whole stall to demand for that one drink and its customers.

items.stem: At a college fest, one stall sells juice and packaged snacks without fruit, while another sells only juice. If fruit prices jump, which stall has another line?

options.text: The juice-and-snacks stall.
options.feedback: A separate product gives it one source of sales that does not use the costly fruit.

options.text: The juice-only stall.
options.feedback: All its sales still depend on juice, so a fruit cost shock reaches its sole line.

items.stem: A portfolio holds four firms that all need the same crop. That crop fails. About how many holdings are shielded just because the company names differ?

options.text: 0 holdings.
options.feedback: All four share the crop risk. Different names alone do not shield any holding from that shock.

options.text: 3 holdings.
options.feedback: The crop can hurt all four. Separate names do not make three holdings safe.

items.stem: A student holds shares in four firms that all rely on the same crop. What risk remains?

options.text: A crop shock can hurt all four.
options.feedback: All four firms need the crop. One bad harvest could hurt each of them.

options.text: There is no shared risk at all.
options.feedback: The firms may be separate, yet one poor harvest can affect all of them.

items.stem: One holding fails while the others keep value. Why does spreading money help here but not promise safety from every shock?

options.text: The failure reaches only part of the mix.
options.feedback: Other holdings can cushion one firm’s loss, while a shared shock may still reach several.

options.text: Each holding cancels every other holding’s loss.
options.feedback: Separate names do not guarantee opposite price moves when the same event affects them.

items.stem: A mix of holdings can limit one firm's harm. What kind of loss can still hit the whole mix?

options.text: Losses that hit many holdings together.
options.feedback: A broad shock can move several assets at once even when no single firm dominates.

options.text: All links between holdings.
options.feedback: Shared markets and sectors can still connect prices across a mixed set.

items.stem: A portfolio holds ten firms that all need the same crop. A student calls it fully protected because the names differ. What risk remains?

options.text: A crop shock could hurt all ten.
options.feedback: Many firms can share one driver, so their losses can arrive together.

options.text: Equal amounts remove any shared crop risk.
options.feedback: Equal weights limit one firm’s share but cannot erase a shock common to every firm.

items.stem: How can a mixed set still lose value?

options.text: It limits some single-part risk, not every loss.
options.feedback: The mix matters because weak parts may differ, while a common shock can still hurt all.

options.text: It removes all chance of a fall.
options.feedback: Broad market moves can reach many parts of a mix at the same time.

misconceptions.name: One basket is enough
misconceptions.correction: One firm or sector leaves a lot tied to one outcome.

misconceptions.name: Many means no loss
misconceptions.correction: Many holdings can still fall at the same time.

concepts.title: What a stock is
concepts.hook: One share can make a student a tiny owner of a company, yet it does not give a fixed coupon or a promised dividend.
concepts.rule: A share is a small ownership claim in a company. Its price can change; a dividend may be paid, but neither a gain nor a dividend is assured.

claims.text: A share gives part ownership of a company.
A firm may pay a share of its gains. The payout is not sure.

items.stem: At a family shop lesson, Asha gets one share in a firm. What does that piece stand for?

options.text: A small ownership claim.
options.feedback: Ownership can link its value to the firm, while future price and payouts remain uncertain.

options.text: A fixed loan to the firm.
options.feedback: A share is an equity claim; a loan is a different kind of promise.

items.stem: During a hostel quiz, a firm reports no dividend this year. Does a shareholder stop being an owner?

options.text: No; ownership remains.
options.feedback: A dividend is a possible payout, not the test for whether a share represents ownership.

options.text: Yes; no dividend cancels the share.
options.feedback: A firm may retain profit or pay none without turning its shares into nonownership.

items.stem: A student owns 5 of a company’s 100 equal shares. The market price per share halves, but no shares are issued or sold. About what percent of the shares does she still own?

options.feedback: A price fall changes the holding’s market value, not the fraction of unchanged shares she owns.
Halving the price does not halve the number of shares or the ownership fraction.

items.stem: A cricket club sells a ticket and issues an ownership share. Which gives a claim on the club itself?

options.text: The ownership share.
options.feedback: The share links the holder to the enterprise; a ticket grants a service instead.

options.text: The one-match ticket.
options.feedback: Entry to one event is not the same as holding a slice of the organisation.

items.stem: A company pays a dividend, yet its share price falls. Why is this possible for an owner?

options.text: Market price and dividend are separate outcomes.
options.feedback: Ownership can bring a dividend without guaranteeing what later buyers will pay for the share.

options.text: Any dividend locks the price above the old price.
options.feedback: A cash payment to owners does not force the market price to stay up.

items.stem: A company may pay owners some profit. That possible payment is called a ___.

options.text: Dividend.
options.feedback: It can transfer part of profit to owners, but a firm need not declare one.

options.text: Guaranteed interest coupon.
options.feedback: Fixed loan interest belongs to debt terms; shares do not promise that coupon.

items.stem: A company paid a dividend last year. A student writes the same monthly payout into this year’s budget. What is the weak step?

options.text: Past dividends do not guarantee new ones.
options.feedback: The firm may pay less, or nothing. Owning shares does not promise cash each month.

options.text: A prior dividend creates a fixed monthly debt.
options.feedback: Shares are ownership claims, so a past payout is not a promise of a repeated payment.

items.stem: Which line could a student use to explain a share?

options.text: It is ownership with an uncertain price and possible dividends.
options.feedback: The two ways to get a return can vary, and neither is built in as a guarantee.

options.text: It is a loan repaid at a fixed date.
options.feedback: A share does not have the fixed repayment promise that defines a loan.

misconceptions.name: Share is a loan
misconceptions.correction: A share is ownership, not a fixed loan payment.

misconceptions.name: Dividend is owed
misconceptions.correction: A firm may pay a dividend; it is not automatic.
